mainEntity.name: Is it normal to have sensitive teeth after getting veneers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is common to experience some degree of tooth sensitivity after veneer placement. This occurs because a thin layer of enamel is removed during preparation, bringing the dentine closer to the surface. Dentine contains microscopic channels connected to the tooth nerve, making it more reactive to temperature and pressure. In most cases, sensitivity gradually reduces over the first one to two weeks. Using a toothpaste formulated for sensitive teeth can help. If sensitivity is severe or worsening, consult your dentist for further assessment.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to get used to the feel of new veneers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most patients adapt to the feel of their new veneers within the first one to two weeks. Initially, you may notice your tongue frequently exploring the new surfaces, and your bite may feel slightly different. As your muscles, jaw, and sensory awareness adjust, these feelings typically subside. The aesthetic change can also take a little getting used to — it is normal to need a short period of adjustment to your new smile. If bite discomfort persists beyond two weeks, contact your dentist.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally during the first week after veneer placement?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can eat most foods, but it is sensible to avoid very hard, crunchy, or sticky items during the first few days while the adhesive fully sets and your teeth are settling. Biting directly into hard foods with the veneered teeth — such as crusty bread or hard raw vegetables — is best avoided. Very hot or cold foods may exacerbate sensitivity temporarily. Eating a slightly softer diet in the early days and returning to your normal routine gradually is generally advisable.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my veneer feels loose or comes off?

acceptedAnswer.text: If a veneer feels loose or becomes dislodged, contact your dental practice as soon as possible. Do not attempt to reattach it yourself. Keep the veneer safe — wrapped in a clean tissue or small container — and bring it with you to your appointment. Your dentist can assess whether it can be rebonded or whether further treatment is required. A loose veneer is not considered a dental emergency in most cases, but it should be attended to promptly to protect the prepared tooth beneath.

mainEntity.name: Will my gums bleed after veneer placement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some very minor gum irritation or slight bleeding when brushing immediately after veneer placement can occur, particularly around the veneer margins. This is usually a result of gentle gum manipulation during the procedure and settles quickly with consistent but gentle oral hygiene. If gum bleeding is more significant, persists beyond the first week, or is accompanied by swelling or pain, you should contact your dental practice to arrange a review. Good hygiene supports gum healing effectively during this period.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if something is wrong after getting veneers?

acceptedAnswer.text: While mild sensitivity and gum tenderness are normal in the first week, certain signs suggest that professional assessment may be needed. These include persistent or worsening pain, a veneer that feels loose or has come away, significant bite imbalance causing jaw pain, visible swelling of the gum or surrounding tissue, or any unusual appearance of the tooth or veneer. Trust your instincts — if something feels significantly wrong or is causing you genuine concern, contacting your dental practice is always the right course of action.
